figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: NorthCUA-Pro performance compared with leading models.
figures.headline: NorthCUA-Pro is compared with leading models on the reported benchmarks, with the family placed highest among open-source models.
citing_sentences: The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings (Figure 1).
NorthCUA establishes state-of-the-art results among open-source models in all three domains (Figure 1).
We select the six benchmarks in Figure 1 to cover these complementary requirements.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The NorthCUA experience loop. 01 The harness executes desktop and web tasks, records their trajectories, and retains workspaces through required live inspection. 02 The Experience Flywheel expands intents, environments, and verifiers into executable tasks, then curates assessed trajectories. The hard-task panel denotes skill-guided and checkpoint-assisted collection through the harness (Section 4.3). 03 Staged Learning converts complementary experience into an updated policy for subsequent execution. GUI states, cursor cues, and rewards are schematic. Trajectory rows omit intermediate actions, and GRPO retains valid failures alongside successes.
figures.headline: The experience loop connects harness execution, Experience Flywheel curation, and Staged Learning, feeding an updated policy back to execution.
citing_sentences: We connect executable tasks to policy updates through three components (Figure 2), focusing on GUI-based software operation.
Shared task, execution, and assessment interfaces connect these learning stages to experience collection (Figure 2).
The experience loop in Figure 2 connects task construction to execution and learning.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Task scope and interaction. (a) Single-step grounding predicts a target location in a fixed screenshot. The enlarged output view marks the zoom tool, with absolute pixel coordinates in the original image. (b) Desktop and web agents change software state through successive actions, with completion assessed from the resulting artifacts or state. Web observations also include DOM information. Generated GUI scenes, action overlays, and outcomes are illustrative. The displayed transitions omit intermediate interactions.
figures.headline: Grounding predicts a target location in a fixed screenshot, while desktop and web tasks are judged from resulting artifacts or software state.
citing_sentences: We study two capability targets in desktop and web environments (Figure 3): locating a requested control in a screenshot and completing a task through software interaction.
The query can describe the element’s appearance or function, such as locating the zoom tool in Figure 3(a).
Figure 3(b) illustrates the two interaction settings:

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: NorthCUA Harness lifecycle. Within the expanded attempt, the shared runtime and long-horizon support sustain GUI interaction while retaining the full trajectory. The evaluator inspects recorded behavior and the live environment. Trajectory, task artifacts, evaluation results, and task metadata are saved in an experience record before the workspace is released. The lower lanes show parallel instances of this lifecycle, coordinated by the batch collection service. GUI scenes, agent imagery, and trajectories are illustrative.
figures.headline: Each harness attempt is kept inspectable, with its trajectory, outputs, and evaluation saved before the workspace is released.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 organizes this lifecycle at two levels.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Context for long-horizon execution. The complete trajectory is retained separately from the next-action context. The visual window contains historical pre-action overlays and the latest clean tool-result image. Textual action and result history can outlast image eviction until compaction. Compaction summarizes earlier actions and results, omits old GUI locators, and preserves recent complete exchanges and the current GUI. An active agent-written note carries the overdue total from workbook to report. PDF export remains unconfirmed. GUI scenes and the displayed visual-window size are illustrative, with intermediate interactions omitted.
figures.headline: Compaction keeps earlier actions as text and recent exchanges with the current screen, while the full trajectory is stored separately.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 follows one invoice workflow across these mechanisms.
The right-hand panel of Figure 5 shows this transfer: note N1 records the overdue total from the workbook for later use in the report.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Action-aware visual feedback. Matched crops show the historical pre-action view with its NorthCUA overlay (left) and the clean resulting state (right). 01 A click opens the chart dialog. 02 A drag moves a video clip earlier on its track. 03 Scrolling reveals route details below. 04 A text badge records the payload entered into the focused field. Screenshots come from interactive GUI mockups with generated scenery. Overlays use the unmodified runtime renderer. The input badge is enlarged below its historical view.
figures.headline: Historical screenshots carry overlays for clicks, drags, scrolls, and typed input, so each pre-action view can be compared with its clean result.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 6, a click marker locates the control that opens a dialog, a drag path links the clip’s old and new positions, and a scroll cue identifies the direction in which the page moved.
Figure 6 pairs each annotated pre-action view with its clean resulting state to make the operation and observed change easy to compare.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Agentic outcome evaluation. Open questions guide selective retrieval and live inspection in the task environment. E1 records an issued export, E2 establishes file presence, and E3 exposes PDF contents for comparison with the source workbook. Unresolved questions prompt further checks and can remain unresolved in the final report. Evidence-linked findings distinguish task fulfillment from execution assessment. GUI views, tool results, actions, and findings are illustrative. Generated document views are cropped, intermediate actor actions are omitted, and selected quality fields are shown without ratings.
figures.headline: The evaluator checks an export's recorded action, file presence, and PDF contents, reporting task fulfillment separately from execution quality.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 shows how recorded work and active inspection together support an evidence-linked assessment.
In Figure 7’s export example, the evaluator checks that the PDF exists and opens it to compare its contents with the source.
Figure 7’s report separates completion from execution quality so that these dimensions can be used together in selection.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Batch rollout at scale. (a) A centralized controller manages agent runners connected to device workers in independent E2B sandboxes over long-lived WebSocket connections. Each worker shares its sandbox’s lifecycle. (b) Staggered lifecycles overlap preparation, execution, and evaluation. Ready intervals mark prepared environments awaiting dispatch. Sandboxes remain available through live checks and output capture. Record icons mark captured outputs that persist after release. The vertical time slice marks concurrent stages. Timings and concurrency are schematic, and GUI scenes are generated illustrations.
figures.headline: Batch rollout runs isolated sandboxes under a central controller, with staggered lifecycles overlapping preparation, execution, and evaluation.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows the two relationships behind this design.
We therefore separate centralized agent control from device execution, as shown in Figure 8(a):
Figure 8(b) makes this overlap visible in the offset Prepare blocks.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Constructing GUI grounding examples. (a) Screenshots cover public UI datasets, web-collected interfaces, and states encountered in agent trajectories. (b) Visual annotations and available accessibility metadata describe one target in its original screenshot. (c) Name-, position-, and operation-based queries each form a separate candidate example with the same clean screenshot and absolute target point. The enlarged Day–Week–Month control group supplies the local evidence for these descriptions. GUI assets are illustrative. Target outlines explain construction, while training uses the unmarked $1536\times 1024$ source image.
figures.headline: Grounding examples are built from screenshots and interface metadata, with several queries per control sharing one target coordinate.
citing_sentences: We use screenshot evidence and available interface metadata to describe visible controls across diverse applications and states (Figure 9).
We use the three-step procedure in Figure 9.
For the calendar example in Figure 9(b), the record identifies the blue Week tab between Day and Month, together with a point inside its clickable region.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Documentation-guided control disambiguation. (a) The screenshot supplies the application, version, and located target. (b) Online manual search retrieves control images and descriptions for visual top-$k$ candidates. One aligns the left edges of separate objects, while the other aligns paragraph text within a fixed text object. (c) Panel and selection context determine the function match, which guides query generation. Each query retains the original screenshot and target point. The GUI, documentation cards, and before/after operation diagrams are illustrative. Documentation supports sample construction.
figures.headline: Documentation lookup resolves an ambiguous alignment icon to its documented function, which then guides the query for the located control.
citing_sentences: We retrieve application knowledge when a control’s appearance leaves its function unclear, then use the matched function to generate queries (Figure 10).
Figure 10 illustrates three steps.
In Figure 10, object alignment and paragraph alignment provide plausible visual candidates.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Three task-construction routes. Scaling Intents binds functions to file or website content before writing requests. Scaling Environments prepares files and applications for sourced requests or reconstructs website interfaces and backing state from references. Scaling Verifiers jointly adapts requests, setup, and executable checks, then tests tasks and verifiers. Each alternative route produces a complete task binding a request, environment setup, and outcome assessment. GUI trials test completion from the initial state, while result probes test acceptance of correct outcomes and rejection of incorrect ones. GUI assets and task packages are illustrative.
figures.headline: Three construction routes start from different resources, but each produces a complete task with a request, workspace setup, and outcome assessment.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 compares three construction routes by what they start with and what they generate:

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: A concrete executable task contract. The saved commercial-review CaseSpec binds a request, input files, startup, and output collection. The initial-workspace illustration redraws representative source records in Calc. Requested deliverables comprise a refreshable dashboard, an editable two-page memo with PDF export, and an editable four-slide review deck. Inspection requirements summarize the query, while post-run collection gathers available files for assessment. GUI views, requested output layouts, abbreviated filenames, and the launch command are illustrative.
figures.headline: A saved commercial-review task binds a request, input files, startup instructions, and output collection to a set of checkable deliverables.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 shows one saved commercial-review task: its request asks for a quarterly comparison, its workbook and startup instructions establish the initial Calc workspace, and its requirements specify the deliverables and how they should agree.
The dashboard, memo, and review deck in Figure 12 are outputs the agent is asked to create.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Constructing a desktop base task. The selected Calc function narrows compatible workbooks. The orders.xlsx summary grounds the Status = Pending condition, while the persona guides request wording. CaseSpec binds this request and file to startup instructions and the required saved filter. The required view retains A17 and A58 and hides A42 without deleting source rows. Software and GUI assets, records, and setup are illustrative. The right-hand view specifies a requirement, not an observed rollout.
figures.headline: A desktop base task is built from a workbook and a selected function, producing a saved filter that hides nonmatching rows without deleting them.
citing_sentences: Figure 13 illustrates the three steps used to generate the request.
Figure 13 uses matched views of the initial workbook and the required saved filter, which hides nonmatching rows without deleting them.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Constructing long-horizon tasks from blueprints. (1) Blueprint selection assembles work stages and prerequisites. Solid edges carry content dependencies. The dashed C-to-D edge sets workflow order. A node can require several GUI actions. (2) Materials bind the approved amount and obsolete wording to inclusion and exclusion conditions for D’s PDF. C binds an initial record to the required budget-decision update. (3) The grounded plan guides LLM request writing and supplies the workspace and outcome requirements in one CaseSpec. Its two outputs are the PDF and updated record. Discovery facts remain in the prepared files. The structure follows a saved plan. GUI details, the shortened request, and prospective outcomes are illustrative.
figures.headline: Long-horizon tasks are assembled from blueprint stages whose content and workflow dependencies are bound into one executable task specification.
citing_sentences: The procedure in Figure 14 has three steps.
Figure 14(1) shows an office-delivery example of this planning process.
The office sample follows this path in Figure 14(2).

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Request-driven desktop environment construction. EnvAgent identifies the required resources, retrieves an order table, and uses its identifiers to construct a missing shipment table. An LLM grounds the sourced request in the prepared filenames and their shared Order ID field. EnvAgent specifies startup and checks the materials and preparation plan, revising inputs or instructions when checks fail before producing a CaseSpec. The GUI agent subsequently performs the requested comparison. GUI views and records are illustrative.
figures.headline: Request-driven construction uses EnvAgent to build a missing shipment table from order identifiers, so the sourced request matches the prepared files.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 illustrates three construction steps.
Figure 15(2) shows an example of this step.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Reconstructing interactive websites from references. The aligned GUI views follow record R17 from the reference site to the local implementation and a reload test. Observed pages and interactions guide the interface and shared backing record. The test edits and saves the title, then reloads the record to check persistence. Discrepancies return to implementation for repair and retesting. The checked site is packaged with its declared initial records and runtime configuration, separately from construction-test edits. GUI states and URLs are illustrative.
figures.headline: Interactive websites are reconstructed from references and checked by a reload test confirming that an edited title persists in the backing record.
citing_sentences: Our URL-to-environment construction builds on WebAnything (Xie et al., 2026) and follows the four steps in Figure 16.
Figure 16(3) shows a persistence test on record R17.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Browser interaction guides iterative code repair. (1) The issue fixes the expected behavior. (2) The Coding Agent inspects and edits the relevant implementation, then launches a candidate application. (3) The Web Test Agent edits R17, saves the new title, and reloads the page. The stacked views show the new title after saving and the old title after reload, with cursor overlays marking interactions. A test report returns this discrepancy, recorded actions, and screenshots to the Coding Agent for repair and retesting under the unchanged expectation. Generated GUI views, code, and test feedback are illustrative.
figures.headline: Browser testing feeds a discrepancy report back to the coding step, which repairs the site and is retested under the same expectation.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 shows how browser testing guides successive code revisions.
These actions, illustrated by the editor views in Figure 17(2), supply a runnable candidate whose behavior still needs to be tested.
The stacked views in Figure 17(3) follow the same R17 record through editing, saving, and reloading.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Bug-guided repair and targeted retesting. Desktop and narrow-screen tests produce one report, which guides both code changes before retesting. Screenshots are later replays of archived code, with subtitle line breaks cleaned for presentation. Overlays, report excerpts, and abbreviated patches are explanatory. R2 passed three selected checks, including homepage appearance, without repeating all five R1 items.
figures.headline: Desktop and narrow-screen test findings guide code changes, and the retest repeats only selected checks rather than all original items.
citing_sentences: Figure 18 follows a local Mercedes-Benz GLE SUV homepage built from supplied materials.
The development case in Figure 18, separate from the scored WebTestBench evaluation, illustrates how such findings can guide a test–repair–retest cycle.
The main-text case in Figure 18 records browser testing and code repair during local-page development.

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: Expanding tasks and their verifiers together. The agent extracts a subtask, changes a selection criterion, or joins approval with export, adapting completion and preservation checks to the new task. The lower composition example separates a GUI execution trial from verifier tests on prepared outcomes. The verdict column gives the requirement-derived response for each probe. Testing checks whether the verifier returns it. The task lists, generated GUI views, and hypothetical judgments illustrate the construction procedure. The ellipsis omits intervening GUI actions, including export. Initial-state preparation and repair iterations are not shown.
figures.headline: Expanding a task also changes its verifier, with each request variant paired with completion and preservation checks adapted to match.
citing_sentences: Figure 19 illustrates the construction and validation phases.
The approval example in Figure 19 shows the effect of each choice on the requested work and the corresponding outcome checks.
The lower part of Figure 19 keeps these two sources of evidence separate.

figures.label: Figure 20
figures.caption: Accumulating operating knowledge through exploration. The source report contains “Quarterly,” but an image-only export makes the phrase unsearchable in the PDF. Further exploration yields a text-preserving procedure. An agent follows its fixed instructions in a separate trial and searches the resulting PDF. The validated skill then guides a new attempt in the original workspace, where full-task checks determine trajectory acceptance. The return arrow depicts a failed task attempt, while failed validation also prompts revision. Accepted trajectories retain the supplied skill in context. GUI scenes, controls, actions, and outcomes are illustrative, with intermediate exploratory trials omitted.
figures.headline: Exploration turns an unsearchable image-only export into a tested text-preserving procedure, which then guides a new attempt in the original workspace.
citing_sentences: Skill-guided recursive exploration turns trial-and-error findings into tested procedures that guide subsequent attempts (Figure 20).
We design a skill-guided loop with four stages, shown in Figure 20.
In the representative report workflow in Figure 20, exploration may reveal several export options.

figures.label: Figure 21
figures.caption: Retaining progress for branching trajectory search. Checkpoint M2 pairs the prepared report and software state with the agent context. Independent continuations restore this checkpoint to try different exports. The example contrasts image-only, text-preserving, and incomplete single-page exports. The lower panel retains the common prefix and the chosen continuation as one candidate path. The original task verifier checks the PDF, earlier record update, and source preservation before accepting the trajectory. Failed continuations leave the parent available for further attempts. GUI states and diagnostic outcomes are illustrative.
figures.headline: Milestone checkpoints let independent continuations try different exports from the same software state, with failed branches leaving the parent available.
citing_sentences: Milestone-guided trajectory search preserves completed work and resumes exploration from the corresponding software state and agent context (Figure 21).
Figure 21 illustrates how this process builds successful continuations on retained progress.
For the office workflow in Figure 21, the original goal includes updating a business record and producing a searchable PDF.

figures.label: Figure 22
figures.caption: Skill refinement in the TERRA dashboard case. Numbered annotations track chart orientation (1) and series colors (2) through exploration, revised guidance, and a fresh attempt. Attempt 1 repairs the orientation during execution but fails the final palette check. Attempt 2 applies skill v2 and passes all 26 final checks. Chart crops and the final PDF come from recorded artifacts. Window frames and equivalent Python excerpts are composed for presentation.
figures.headline: A revised skill fixes the chart palette in a fresh attempt, which then passes all 26 final checks.
citing_sentences: The TERRA dashboard case in Section 4.3.3 follows how a charting problem becomes revised guidance that a fresh attempt applies (Figure 22).
Figure 22 starts with a request to build a quarterly operations dashboard for TERRA from sales records and store targets.

figures.label: Figure 23
figures.caption: Milestone-guided construction of ORBIT BOTANICA. Three display milestones group the recorded checks. Teal frames mark one retained path, and arrows preserve ancestry through omitted intermediate steps. Branches can complete later work early. The equipped checkpoint and its failed finishing continuation share the unchanged opaque-glass render. Both successful finishing branches pass the full-task checks. Scene crops are unretouched, with frames and diagnostic annotations added for presentation.
figures.headline: Milestone-guided construction keeps checked intermediate states, so later trials revise only the unresolved finishing requirements of a 3D cafe scene.
citing_sentences: A construction case in Section 4.3.3 follows this accumulation of progress from an empty Blender scene to a complete collected trajectory (Figure 23).
Figure 23 follows a request to build ORBIT BOTANICA, a futuristic greenhouse cafe, from an empty Blender scene and deliver an editable model with its final render.

figures.label: Figure 24
figures.caption: Joint desktop–web agentic reinforcement learning. The manager selects tasks, binds verifiers, and prepares isolated environments. Workers use a model checkpoint to act through desktop or web interfaces. Manager-run checks supply outcomes before workspace release. The adapter binds outcomes to training samples while preserving each recorded input–response pair and task/attempt identity. The learner uses GRPO to compare valid attempts within the same task, initial-state, and verifier group, then returns an updated checkpoint to workers. Worker and learner icons denote execution and training uses of the same model. GUI scenes and binary outcomes are illustrative. The example leaves task-group size unspecified.
figures.headline: Tasks, verifiers, and worker rollouts feed group-relative updates that return an improved checkpoint to the same workers.
citing_sentences: Figure 24 follows an attempt from task preparation to a policy update.

figures.label: Figure 25
figures.caption: Context-preserving RL sample construction. (a) The earlier input contains Overview and Editing. Appending the typing result preserves history, so Enter title and Save share one segment. After the successful Save action, Overview leaves the visual window (cross), starting a new segment. The highlighted label marks the latest observation. Gray objects supply context, while teal responses and token spans contribute to policy loss. (b) Task-group outcomes determine one advantage per attempt, shared across its segments. In the trajectory-mean configuration, masked policy losses are pooled and normalized over each attempt’s target tokens before averaging across attempts (Eq. 1). Panel (a) shows one continuous attempt under one behavior-policy version, with earlier images unchanged until eviction. GUI states, responses, and outcomes are illustrative. Thumbnails are input excerpts, strip lengths are schematic, and earlier calls are omitted.
figures.headline: Input preservation keeps one continuous attempt as a single segment until old screenshots leave the window, and attempt-level advantages are shared across its segments.
citing_sentences: Figure 25 illustrates input preservation in panel (a) and attempt-level comparison and aggregation in panel (b).
In Figure 25b, the two segments of attempt 1 share $A_{1}$, while attempt 2 receives $A_{2}$.

figures.label: Figure 26
figures.caption: Grounding a documented control. Left, an actual documentation-grounded annotation pairs an Ample Bass P control with its manual-defined articulation and a generated training query. Right, NorthCUA localizes this control in an SSP screenshot with a different surrounding GUI state, following the recorded query legeto slide. The target’s local appearance and position match the construction view. In the enlarged detail, the teal box marks the reference target and the orange point is the recorded prediction. Enlargements and annotations are reader aids. Documentation is used in data construction, not supplied during direct evaluation.
figures.headline: A documentation-derived query for a virtual instrument control localizes the same control in a screenshot with different surrounding interface state.
citing_sentences: Figure 26 illustrates this construction with the Legato Slide control in Ample Bass P, a virtual instrument hosted in FL Studio.

figures.label: Figure 27
figures.caption: Web success by website scope. The six groups partition all 812 WebArena-Verified tasks using retained attempts. Nano and Mini use SFT checkpoints, while Pro uses RL. Pro exceeds 70% in every single-site group and completes 17 of 48 cross-site tasks. Appendix I gives the selection and group details.
figures.headline: Pro exceeds 70% in every single-site web group and completes 17 of 48 cross-site tasks.
citing_sentences: Figure 27 examines trajectories across six website groups, using Nano and Mini after SFT and Pro after RL.
Mini uses the second evaluation round, matching Figure 27.
Figure 27 includes Mini’s SFT website-level breakdown alongside Nano SFT and Pro RL.

figures.label: Figure 28
figures.caption: Source-paper selection before and after long-horizon SFT. A shared question anchors the two equal-width result views. Agent callouts paraphrase recorded selection and checking decisions. Highlighted filenames show the different Q3 sources, while scores cover each complete attempt. Screenshots are cropped observations before the indexed decisions, with enlarged filenames. The runs use different dataset revisions and OCR settings.
figures.headline: The same OSWorld 2.0 request is compared before and after long-horizon supervised training, showing how the agent selects and verifies its source files.
citing_sentences: Figure 28 compares the same OSWorld 2.0 request in two NorthCUA-Mini runs before and after long-horizon SFT, focusing on how the agent selects and verifies source documents.
The pair in Figure 28 has identical requests but different dataset revisions.

figures.label: Figure 29
figures.caption: Desktop visual-experience delivery profiling. The profile uses a separate desktop workload. (a) Encoded image-tensor bytes as a percentage of raw bytes, calculated from the summed paired counters across 28 batches. The dashed reference is the original representation size. (b) Median and interquartile range of component timings for the same update range. Policy synchronization includes the in-flight wait, so the displayed timings are not additive. Payload sizes exclude non-image fields and transport overhead.
figures.headline: Across 28 batches, encoded image tensors are measured against raw bytes, and component timings show the cost of delivering visual experience.
citing_sentences: Figure 29(b) reports delivery and policy-synchronization timings.

figures.label: Figure 30
figures.caption: Executed trajectories with contrasting task rewards. Both Thunderbird attempts reach Tags view. A hides the entire header, while B disables Get Messages specifically. Native screenshot crops show executed click positions in the middle panels and the state before application closure on the right. A’s first two panels crop one observation. B opens the header menu between those panels. The archived configuration verifier returns rewards 0 and 1. Both attempts belong to one eight-member GRPO group containing five successes and three failures, which determines their advantage signs. They span an asynchronous policy update. This is a within-group reward comparison, not a before/after checkpoint evaluation.
figures.headline: Two Thunderbird attempts reach the same view yet receive rewards 0 and 1, showing the terminal reward separates otherwise similar executions.
citing_sentences: Figure 30 examines what the terminal reward distinguishes in an actual task.

figures.label: Figure 31
figures.caption: Recovering from an unavailable browser action. In a retained Pro evaluation attempt, NorthCUA first attempts to select an unavailable Quarter period. It inspects the dropdown, switches to Month with the exact Q1 date range, and reads the resulting table before answering Sprite. The saved evaluator marks the task successful. Numbered panels show observations before decisions 6, 10, and 12 of a 13-decision attempt, with intermediate actions omitted. Detail views enlarge original control crops, with field labels arranged for readability. The answer at decision 13 and the external evaluator’s success marker are annotations outside the webpage.
figures.headline: A Pro attempt recovers from an unavailable quarter filter by switching to a month range with the exact Q1 dates and answers correctly.
citing_sentences: In the Pro episode in Figure 31, NorthCUA is asked to identify the best-selling brand in the first quarter of 2022.
The browser case in Figure 31 is task 1 in the Pro export.

figures.label: Figure 32
figures.caption: Choice-based Web execution. The input shows the title before editing. Generated GUI views illustrate filling the new title (right) and a subsequent Save click (left). At each decision, current controls support operation and target selection. A direct choice executes without decoding, while a generation route triggers a second full-model call with the original prompt and a fresh cache. Optional LoRA adapters are active only for classification. Route and target checks are omitted.
figures.headline: Each decision either directly selects a control or generates text through a second full-model call, showing how web execution is divided.
citing_sentences: Figure 32 illustrates the resulting division of work.

figures.label: Figure 33
figures.caption: Ultrafast product-update case. Selected Head + LoRA decisions from one WebArena-Verified attempt. Lightning and text-entry icons distinguish direct choice from native generation. Numbers retain the original decision indices, with intermediate steps omitted. Insets enlarge recorded details, with post-action states labeled.
figures.headline: A Head plus LoRA attempt disables a product after a search recovery, with six of twelve executed browser actions taken as direct choices.
citing_sentences: Figure 33 follows a Head + LoRA attempt at a WebArena-Verified task that asks the agent to disable Karmen yoga pants because of quality issues.
Both Ultrafast variants and the case in Figure 33 use the generation-preferred profile with a finite-choice confidence threshold of 0.8.

figures.label: Figure 34
figures.caption: Four states of the same report task. Missing output and missing regional detail should be rejected. A complete table and an equivalent chart should be accepted. Both accepted examples are stipulated to satisfy the full contract, including regional discussion, template compliance, and unchanged source files. The GUI excerpts and inspection asset are illustrative. The dashed red region annotates missing content. Accept/Reject labels show the expected verdicts for these illustrative states.
figures.headline: Four report states show that missing output or regional detail is rejected, while a complete table and an equivalent chart are accepted.
citing_sentences: Figure 34 gives a concrete regional-report example.

figures.label: Figure 35
figures.caption: A persistence example for evidence qualification. The new title appears after saving but reverts after a completed reload. The report preserves this mismatch for repair. An interrupted save or reload requires diagnosis and retesting before assigning a product defect. Final acceptance uses fixed checks in a fresh state outside the repair loop. GUI states and inspection materials illustrate the proposed protocol.
figures.headline: A title edit appears after saving but reverts after reload, so the report keeps the mismatch for diagnosis before assigning a product defect.
citing_sentences: Figure 35 uses a title-persistence requirement to make this decision concrete.

figures.caption: NorthCUA case study in GeoGebra. The trajectory connects expression entry to geometry, playback, and parameter checks. The first construction is enlarged from state 79. Panel 6 compares depths 0.20 and 0.65 at fixed pulse phase 0 and slice position $-0.8$. The section detail enlarges state 429. Numbers identify captured states in row order. Editorial overlays summarize nearby actions, with intervening actions omitted.
figures.headline: A GeoGebra trajectory moves from expression entry to geometry, playback, and parameter checks across numbered captured states.
citing_sentences: Figure 36 begins with an empty workspace.

figures.caption: NorthCUA case study in Calc and LabPlot. Repeat-aware classification supplies the temperature maps and derived plots. citing_sentences: In Figure 37, the agent imports 2,142 sweep rows into Calc and fills formulas that classify 1,071 operating groups.

figures.caption: NorthCUA case study in Calc and Impress. Selected states follow calculation, chart transfer, diagram construction, and data readback. The chart at state 282 has just been inserted and is later resized and positioned. The lower-left inset enlarges the native diagram at state 687, while the large view shows the finished evidence slide at state 688. Enlarged chart and data-table views connect the mean at state 136 to its embedded value at state 649. Numbers identify captured states. Editorial overlays summarize nearby actions.
figures.headline: A Calc and Impress trajectory moves calculated data into a chart and native diagram, ending with an evidence slide.
citing_sentences: Figure 38 starts with an empty presentation and a first cover.

figures.label: Figure 39
figures.caption: NorthCUA case study in Virtuoso and Spectre. Panel 2 pairs device identity and size fields from the same native dialog at state 78. Panel 6 enlarges the crossing at state 318, estimated by interpolation between the 0.495 and 0.500 V sweep samples. Current annotations transcribe the PMOS and NMOS reports at states 335 and 340, respectively, both at nominal input 0.5 V. Numbers identify captured states. Editorial overlays summarize nearby actions, with intervening actions omitted.
figures.headline: A Virtuoso and Spectre trajectory starts from an empty schematic and transcribes PMOS and NMOS reports at nominal 0.5 V.
citing_sentences: Figure 39 begins with an empty schematic.

figures.label: Figure 40
figures.caption: NorthCUA case study in Inkscape and Blender. Twelve selected states trace drawing, modeling, material revision, and camera keying. Panel 2 is the exported sketch. Panels 8 and 12 pair viewport and settings crops from their respective states. Editorial cues summarize nearby actions. abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop–web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings (Figure 1). For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality–latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

sections.body: The paper presents NorthCUA, which links three components. The NorthCUA Harness runs and assesses tasks, the Experience Flywheel constructs tasks and curates verified trajectories, and Staged Learning trains the policy on that experience. Shared execution and outcome interfaces let the updated policy return for fresh attempts. The family has Nano (9B), Mini (35B), and Pro (397B) sizes, built on Qwen3.5. Pro outperforms Qwen3.8-Max and Kimi-K3 on both grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified. Mini surpasses Kimi-K3 on OSWorld-Verified and Qwen3.8-Max on WebArena-Verified. NorthCUA-Ultrafast completes matched successful WebArena-Verified tasks 2.3× faster on average than full generation.
sections.heading: 1Introduction
sections.headline: NorthCUA couples executable task construction, agent execution, and policy training so experience from software use feeds back into the policy.

sections.body: Two capability targets are evaluated separately. Single-step UI grounding takes a screenshot and a natural-language query and makes one prediction of the target element's coordinates. End-to-end computer use combines a fixed user request, an initial software environment, and conditions for judging completion. The agent observes the current state, takes an action, and uses the feedback to choose its next step. Desktop agents use desktop screenshots with mouse and keyboard actions. Web agents use page screenshots and DOM information with browser tools. Both follow the same observation, action, and feedback loop. Each executable task is packaged as a CaseSpec and assessed against its declared requirements to select demonstrations.
sections.heading: 2Scope and System Overview
sections.headline: The paper separates single-step control grounding from end-to-end desktop and web tasks, each with fixed requests and completion checks.

sections.body: The Agent Kit separates a shared ReAct-style runtime from platform adapters, so desktop and web agents reuse model invocation, context management, and trajectory recording. Sessions, rounds, and steps track persistent application state, individual requests, and single decisions. For context, a sliding window keeps up to $k$ recent frames with action overlays, task-preserving compaction summarizes earlier progress, and structured working memory holds facts the agent retains. The complete trajectory is stored separately from the decision context. The Batch Rollout Service runs each attempt in an isolated E2B sandbox under a centralized controller, prepares upcoming environments in advance, and applies stage-specific concurrency limits. Recovery checks whether an attempt is still running or completed before retrying evaluation or rerunning the task in a fresh environment.
sections.heading: 3NorthCUA Harness: Full-Lifecycle Infrastructure for Computer Use
sections.headline: The NorthCUA Harness runs each attempt through a shared runtime, long-horizon context management, outcome evaluation, and batch collection with preserved records.

sections.body: Grounding examples come from two routes. The broad route collects screenshots from public UI datasets, web-collected interfaces, and agent trajectories, parses controls with OmniParser, and adds accessibility metadata when available. The documentation route retrieves application manuals when a control's function is unclear, then matches documented illustrations to the screenshot. Both produce screenshot, query, and coordinate records that pass geometry and multimodal correctness checks, followed by deduplication and selection. For full tasks, Scaling Intents, Scaling Environments, and Scaling Verifiers bind requests, workspaces, and executable checks. Hard tasks use skill-guided exploration and milestone-guided search, which keep validated skills and verified checkpoints. The text states that successful trajectories remain scarce for the hardest workflows, the gap these methods address.
sections.heading: 4Experience Flywheel: Scaling Grounding and Agentic Experience
sections.headline: The Experience Flywheel builds grounding examples and executable tasks through three construction routes, and retains progress from hard tasks via skills and milestones.

sections.body: Training runs in three stages on one policy. Broad GUI mid-training uses more than 100,000 trajectories and more than 4,000,000 GUI steps, plus approximately 40,000 single-step grounding examples. Verified long-horizon supervised fine-tuning keeps trajectories whose final results pass the original task verifier, approximately 3,000 trajectories with 310,000 GUI interaction steps. Joint desktop–web reinforcement learning then uses fresh attempts drawn from a prepared task pool, with executable verifiers scoring each attempt. GRPO compares valid attempts within each task group, and all segments of an attempt share one advantage. Asynchronous updates pause new model calls, commit new weights, and resume, so policy lag can affect the resulting update.
sections.heading: 5Staged Learning from Scalable GUI Experience
sections.headline: Staged Learning trains in three stages: broad GUI mid-training, verified long-horizon supervised fine-tuning, and joint desktop–web reinforcement learning.

sections.body: Evaluation covers six benchmarks: ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G for grounding, OSWorld-Verified and OSWorld 2.0 for desktop, and WebArena-Verified and WebTestBench for Web. Grounding results use the long-horizon SFT checkpoints, while desktop and Web results use final RL checkpoints. In the authors' evaluation, Claude Opus 5.5 scores 88.1% and 89.9% on the two grounding benchmarks. On all 812 WebArena-Verified tasks, Full generation reaches 64.2% success. Head + LoRA reaches 60.6% success, with mean task time of 266.8 s against 616.8 s, and bypasses generation for 31.1% of recorded actions. Limitations: Mid already contains NorthCUA training, and some comparison scores are published figures rather than the authors' own runs.
sections.heading: 6Experiments and Analysis
sections.headline: NorthCUA-Pro scores 93.3% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 91.0% on OSWorld-G, the highest among systems compared in grounding.

sections.body: The related work covers three areas. Grounding and policy work includes SeeClick, GUI-Actor, GUI-Cursor, UI-TARS, OpenCUA, ComputerRL, ScaleCUA, and Qwen-CUA. Task and experience construction work includes OS-Genesis, GUI-360, ProCUA-SFT, CUA-Gym, Qwen-UI-Agent, and WEFT. Harness and infrastructure work includes UFO, UFO2, UFO3, Agent Lightning v1.0, Orchard, and Polar. The authors state that their emphasis is on preserving decision-time inputs and weighting complete attempts within the Harness and experience-production pipeline. They also state that NorthCUA focuses on integrating these system responsibilities for stateful visual interaction, rather than on any single component.
sections.heading: 7Related Work
sections.headline: NorthCUA differs from prior systems by integrating decision-time input preservation and complete-attempt weighting with its harness and experience pipeline.

sections.body: The authors name three limits. First, unfamiliar software and changing interface conventions remain challenging, and extending coverage and reliable execution as applications evolve is left as future work. Second, feedback quality depends on predicate coverage and on the calibration of model judgments for open-ended content. Third, long workflows concentrate many decisions into one terminal outcome, which can make credit assignment harder. For deployment, the section lists isolated workspaces, explicit tool profiles, and retained execution records, along with authorized access, least-privilege credentials, and confirmation for consequential actions. It also notes indirect prompt injection from external pages and documents, and calls for licensing, privacy, and credential review of released materials.
sections.heading: 8Limitations and Responsible Use
sections.headline: Open limits include unfamiliar software, verifier coverage, and terminal-only feedback on long workflows.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the three results. Across six benchmarks, the Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves the highest results among open-source models in GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction. At 397B parameters, Pro outperforms the trillion-parameter general-purpose baselines on both grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified. Stage comparisons show gains in desktop and Web execution across all three sizes after long-horizon SFT and joint RL. NorthCUA-Ultrafast is presented as a complementary route to faster decision-making. The authors release the three models, the full Harness code, and the technical report.
sections.heading: 9Conclusion
sections.headline: NorthCUA reports the highest open-source results across three domains and releases its three models and harness code.

sections.body: The appendix gives implementation details. A shared attempt identity links each executable task, its workspace, and its learning samples. Information boundaries separate construction metadata, the acting policy's permitted inputs, and host-only acceptance criteria, and keep actor and evaluator records apart. Grounding and task construction details cover annotation records, dependency checks, environment binding, hard-task checkpoints, and controlled verifier states. Table 16 reports rounded supervised scale, with over 100,000 trajectories and over 4 million GUI interactions for mid-training. Table 17 lists the Qwen3.5 backbone variants. It also covers a web repair protocol and five OSWorld 2.0 execution cases.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists implementation and information boundaries, grounding and task construction details, training data scale, model identities, and extended case studies.
